newsitem.title: UK: POSTCARDS FROM THE FUTURE - only some rats survive.
newsitem.headline: POSTCARDS FROM THE FUTURE - only some rats survive.

text.p: A British-based think tank published three "postcards from the future" on Tuesday, including a grim scenario in which the industrialised world becomes a "rat race where only some rats will survive".

The Royal Institute of International Affairs, looking to the year 2015, said the industrialised world can only succeed if it adapts to the increasing pace of economic, technological and social change.
In a report entitled "Unsettled Times" by the Chatham House Forum, it said the future will challenge many of the fundamental precepts underlying commerce, government and society.
"Strategies set without proper exploration and assessment of these challenges may lead organisations astray," it said.

The report came up with three scenarios for the future which it said were not meant to be taken as predictions but rather as attempts to sketch out plausible alternatives for consideration as a means of planning for what lies ahead.
The first scenario, which it called "Faster, faster", points to a world of starkly accelerating change which perpetually threatens to spin out of control.
In the commercial world, sources of advantage are becoming scarce. There is little advantage from specialisation as there are now numerous ways of achieving the same end.
The report gave the example of wine production, saying modern methods would allow any producers to deliver a taste similar to any chosen vintage provided grapes are grown on reasonable soils.
"In order to keep up, everyone has to run faster, and faster still," the report said. "Those who will not run, or who stumble, suffer huge penalties."
The second scenario, "The Post-Industrial Revolution," promises a kinder, gentler future, which recognises that too much innovation is as bad as too little.
By ensuring companies can remain competitive by profiting from innovations, employees feel a restored sense of competence, operating in an environment they can understand and trust.
Here, the government is like the owner of a shopping mall "working to see what can generate the best environment for the individual shops and thereby generate higher rents".
The last scenario, "Rough Neighbours", foresees the industrialised world plunged into a period of protracted instability by socially unmanageable change.
"As many as four successive generations in some families may never have worked," the report said.

Under the third scenario, the report sees other regions of the world, grouped around the growing economic might of China, making the running while the industrialised world grapples to overcome its problems.

"The re-emergent industrialised world is confronted by the rest of the world on terms unlike those of the previous two centuries. Its authority as the source of competence and progress is greatly weakened."
